issues.legal_issue: The court-appointed environmental committee’s credibility and recommendations were not undermined by unsupported allegations of bias or excess of authority.
material_facts: The committee was assigned defined tasks by the Court and submitted reports pursuant to those tasks.
The committee’s recommendations were within the terms of reference fixed by the Court.
The challenge to the committee’s credibility was not supported by material substantiating the allegations.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the committee’s credibility was untenable, and the issue was closed.
issues.legal_principle: A court-appointed body acting within the tasks assigned to it by the Court is not discredited by unsupported allegations. The committee’s powers and functions had been fixed by the Court’s order of 14 December 2007.

rule.if: court_supervised_environmental_proceeding and court_assigned_committee_tasks and committee_acted_within_mandate and credibility_challenge_unsupported

predicates.court_supervised_environmental_proceedin: The matter is a court-supervised proceeding concerning environmental harm.
predicates.court_assigned_committee_tasks: The Court assigned an investigative or advisory body defined tasks.
predicates.committee_acted_within_mandate: The body acted within the tasks assigned by the Court.
predicates.credibility_challenge_unsupported: A party challenged the body's credibility without supporting the challenge with material evidence.

issues.definition: When a body assigned defined tasks by the Court acts within those tasks and an unsupported challenge is made to its credibility, the body's credibility is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: The Court may use its constitutional remedial jurisdiction to address extraordinary environmental harm where statutory remedies are ineffective and the proposed directions do not conflict with statute.
material_facts: The proceeding sought enforcement of fundamental rights in response to large-scale illegal mining and serious environmental damage.
The reported violations had caused extensive harm to forest wealth, ecology, and the national exchequer.
The Court found that the statutory mechanisms would not effectively or adequately address the extraordinary situation.
The proposed measures supplemented the statutory schemes and were not in conflict with them.
issues.conclusion: The Court could exercise its jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 142 to remedy the harm and protect against its continuation, rather than confining the response to statutory remedies.
issues.legal_principle: Article 32 grants broad power to issue appropriate directions for enforcement of fundamental rights, and Article 142 empowers the Court to do complete justice. Article 21 protects the right to life, while Articles 48-A and 51-A(g) reflect environmental protection obligations. Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, (1984) 3 SCC 161, recognizes the breadth of Article 32 and the Court’s ability to devise appropriate procedures; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (1987) 1 SCC 395, recognizes injunctive and remedial power; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (2009) 6 SCC 142, supports intervention to prevent environmental degradation. Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India, (1998) 4 SCC 409, cautions against directly conflicting with statute, but does not prevent supplemental measures in an extraordinary mass-harm situation.

rule.if: fundamental_rights_writ_proceeding and widespread_environmental_harm and statutory_remedies_ineffective and proposed_directions_not_in_statutory_conflict

predicates.fundamental_rights_writ_proceeding: The proceeding seeks judicial enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.widespread_environmental_harm: The alleged conduct caused widespread and serious environmental harm.
predicates.statutory_remedies_ineffective: The available statutory mechanisms would not effectively address the particular scale or urgency of the harm.
predicates.proposed_directions_not_in_statutory_con: The proposed judicial directions supplement, rather than contradict, the governing statutory scheme.

issues.definition: When a fundamental-rights proceeding concerns widespread environmental harm, statutory remedies are ineffective, and proposed directions do not conflict with statute, constitutional remedial jurisdiction may be exercised.

issues.legal_issue: A survey used to determine mining-lease boundaries is reliable where affected leaseholders receive meaningful participation and objections are reconsidered using a technically credible process.
material_facts: Leaseholders or their representatives received advance notice of surveys and could attend them.
Survey teams included representatives of relevant government departments and a technical institution, and the work was supervised by the court-appointed team.
Survey records were shared with leaseholders, who could make representations and receive hearings.
The survey used modern measurement and mapping methods, checked the results against lease sketches and satellite imagery, and allowed corrections after reconsideration of objections.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted the survey findings and the lease boundaries determined on that basis, making those boundaries controlling for the leases involved.
issues.legal_principle: In proceedings under Article 32, the Court may obtain information through a commission or responsible investigative body and determine what weight to give its findings. Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, (1984) 3 SCC 161, explains that such reports can provide prima facie material and that the Court evaluates them alongside objections. Here, the Court found the procedure fair and the technical process credible on the evidence before it.

rule.if: court_supervised_boundary_survey and affected_leaseholders_given_notice_and_participation and objections_reconsidered and survey_method_independently_checked

predicates.court_supervised_boundary_survey: A survey to determine lease boundaries was conducted under court supervision.
predicates.affected_leaseholders_given_notice_and_p: Affected leaseholders received notice and an opportunity to participate in the survey process.
predicates.objections_reconsidered: Objections to the survey findings were reviewed and hearings or corrections were provided where appropriate.
predicates.survey_method_independently_checked: The survey results were checked using technically reliable methods and independent comparisons.

issues.definition: When a court-supervised boundary survey provides affected leaseholders participation, reconsiders objections, and uses independently checked methods, its findings and boundaries are accepted.

issues.legal_issue: Disposal of mining waste as overburden is a mining operation, so the land used for it must be covered by the required mining authority and, if it is forest land, the required forest approval.
material_facts: Leaseholders used land outside their sanctioned lease areas for overburden dumps and related mining activity.
Some of the land used for those purposes was forest land, while other land was non-forest land.
issues.conclusion: Overburden dumping falls within mining operations; forest land used for it requires the requisite forest approval, and non-forest land used for it must be covered by a mining lease.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(d) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 defines mining operations broadly enough to include disposal of mining waste. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 requires approval for use of forest land for non-forest purposes; land used for such activity that is not forest land must be covered by the mining lease.

predicates.mining_activity_proceeding: The dispute concerns the regulation or boundaries of mining activity.
predicates.land_used_for_mining_waste_disposal: Land was used to dispose of waste generated by mining.

issues.definition: When land is used to dispose of mining waste, that disposal is treated as a mining operation.

issues.legal_issue: Classifying mines by the percentage of encroachment in relation to total lease area is not arbitrary where the criterion reasonably identifies the extent of violations and environmental damage.
material_facts: The committee classified leases according to the extent of illegal mining and related encroachment as a percentage of the lease area.
Lease areas varied in size, and an alternative based only on the absolute area encroached would also raise classification concerns.
The Court found the percentage-based criterion reasonably connected to identifying lessees responsible for the greatest violations and environmental damage.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted the classification criterion as reasonable and constitutionally valid.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 requires a classification criterion to avoid hostile discrimination and bear a reasonable nexus to the object sought to be achieved. The existence of a potentially different or supposedly better criterion does not by itself make the adopted criterion arbitrary.

predicates.mine_classification_dispute: The proceeding challenges the classification of mining leases according to the seriousness of violations.
predicates.classification_uses_encroachment_percent: The classification compares the encroached area with the total area of each lease.
predicates.criterion_reasonably_related_to_violatio: The chosen comparison reasonably helps identify the relative seriousness of violations and environmental damage.

issues.definition: When a mine classification uses encroachment as a percentage of lease area and that criterion reasonably reflects violation severity, the criterion is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: Mines with limited or moderate violations may resume operations only after satisfying the applicable statutory, environmental, rehabilitation, and financial conditions imposed for reopening.
material_facts: The Court had permitted some mines with no or marginal illegality to reopen subject to compliance with statutory requirements, satisfactory implementation of rehabilitation measures, and undertakings concerning environmental plans.

Other mines had committed specified illegal mining outside their sanctioned areas and were required to make compensatory payments, provide security for rehabilitation, and contribute a portion of sale proceeds.
The committee recommended reopening further mines only after applicable conditions were met and rehabilitation work was completed or nearing completion to the required satisfaction.
issues.conclusion: The Court approved reopening of the remaining mines in the first category and mines in the second category, subject to the previously imposed conditions and the additional conditions applicable to the latter.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the committee’s recommendations and rehabilitation and reclamation framework as measures for scientific and sustainable mining. It found those conditions consistent with the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. The Court’s orders of 3 September and 28 September 2012 set out the applicable reopening conditions.

rule.if: mining_reopening_proceeding and mine_not_in_highest_violation_class and applicable_statutory_and_environmental_conditions_met and rehabilitation_requirements_satisfied and required_compensation_and_security_provided

predicates.mining_reopening_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether suspended mining operations may resume.
predicates.mine_not_in_highest_violation_class: The mine is not in the class designated for the most serious violations.
predicates.applicable_statutory_and_environmental_c: The operator has met the statutory and environmental conditions applicable to reopening.
predicates.rehabilitation_requirements_satisfied: The required reclamation and rehabilitation measures have been completed or have reached the required stage of implementation.
predicates.required_compensation_and_security_provi: The operator has provided any required compensation, security, or other financial contribution.

issues.definition: When a mine outside the highest-violation class meets its applicable statutory, rehabilitation, and financial conditions, it may resume operations subject to those conditions.

issues.legal_issue: Mines placed in the highest violation class for substantial illegal mining may be closed and their leases cancelled in the public interest.
material_facts: The survey and classification findings identified a class of leases involving substantial illegal mining outside sanctioned areas, including serious encroachment and other flagrant violations.
The Court accepted the survey findings and the rationality of the classification.
The reported violations had caused serious damage to the environment and forest wealth.
issues.conclusion: The Court ordered complete closure and cancellation of leases in the highest violation class, with consequential action under the accepted recommendations; proceeds from sales of their iron ore were to be forfeited to the State and transferred for the designated public purposes.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Article 21 and the principles of inter-generational equity and sustainable development. It balanced public interest, environmental protection, and the need to enforce the law against the individual interests of the most serious violators. The Court accepted the committee’s recommendations concerning cancellation and the subsequent disposition of those leases.

rule.if: illegal_mining_proceeding and substantial_illegal_mining_outside_authorized_area and mine_in_highest_violation_class and serious_environmental_damage

predicates.illegal_mining_proceeding: The proceeding concerns alleged illegal mining and its consequences.
predicates.substantial_illegal_mining_outside_autho: The operator carried out substantial mining outside the area authorized for its operations.
predicates.mine_in_highest_violation_class: The mine was placed in the classification reserved for the most serious violations.
predicates.serious_environmental_damage: The violations caused serious environmental or ecological damage.

issues.definition: When substantial unauthorized mining causes serious environmental damage and places a mine in the highest-violation class, the mine is closed and its lease is cancelled.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on granting new mining leases need not continue where new grants can be considered under law and consistently with the Court’s directions.
material_facts: An earlier order had barred the grant of fresh mining leases.
The Court accepted recommendations for a process to assign areas of cancelled leases to eligible end users through a transparent process.
The Court found no need to continue the general embargo and directed that new grants and pending applications be dealt with according to law and its directions.
issues.conclusion: The general embargo on fresh mining leases was not continued; new grants and pending applications were to be considered in accordance with law and the Court’s directions.
issues.legal_principle: A continuing judicial restriction is not required when the circumstances and accepted remedial framework no longer justify it. Any grant must remain subject to the governing law and the Court’s directions and their purpose.

rule.if: mining_lease_grant_proceeding and earlier_general_embargo_exists and circumstances_no_longer_justify_embargo and lawful_grant_framework_available

predicates.mining_lease_grant_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the grant of new mining leases or the treatment of pending applications.
predicates.earlier_general_embargo_exists: A prior judicial order generally prohibited new lease grants.
predicates.circumstances_no_longer_justify_embargo: Developments in the proceeding mean that the prior general prohibition is no longer considered necessary.
predicates.lawful_grant_framework_available: New grants can be considered under law and in a manner consistent with the Court’s directions.

issues.definition: When a prior general embargo is no longer justified and lawful grants can be considered consistently with court directions, the embargo is not continued.

issues.legal_issue: Mining operations near an unresolved boundary between two states must remain suspended until the boundary is settled and the leases can be reconsidered.
material_facts: Several leases were situated on or near an interstate boundary that had not been finalized.
The states agreed that the boundary would be determined with the assistance of the designated national surveying authority.
The Court found that operations in those leases could not resume until the boundary issue was resolved.
issues.conclusion: Operations in the affected leases remained suspended pending finalization of the interstate boundary, after which resumption could be considered afresh.
issues.legal_principle: Where the location of a lease relative to an unresolved interstate boundary affects its survey and legality, operations should remain suspended until the boundary is determined and the leases can be assessed on the settled boundary.

predicates.mining_lease_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether operations under mining leases may continue.
predicates.lease_near_unsettled_interstate_boundary: A lease lies on or near a boundary between two states that has not been settled.
predicates.lease_location_depends_on_boundary_resol: The lease’s location or status cannot be reliably determined until the boundary is finalized.

issues.definition: When a lease’s status depends on an unsettled interstate boundary, operations remain suspended until the boundary is resolved.

issues.legal_issue: Iron ore from resumed operations may continue to be sold through the court-supervised process, and sub-grade ore in waste dumps may be removed and sold only if the removal is commercially viable and environmentally safe.
material_facts: The Court had directed the sale of accumulated iron ore through an e-auction conducted by a monitoring body.
The committee reported that little sub-grade ore remained and that removing some dumps could threaten vegetation or dump stability.
The committee sought authority to remove and sell sub-grade ore only where commercially worthwhile and environmentally safe.
issues.conclusion: The Court continued the existing court-supervised sale process for iron ore from resumed operations and accepted conditional removal and sale of sub-grade ore where commercially viable and not likely to cause significant environmental harm.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the committee’s recommendations for continued supervised sale and for conditional removal of sub-grade ore, taking account of commercial viability and environmental safety. The sale and monitoring arrangements were based on the Court’s earlier orders and the committee’s report.

rule.if: court_supervised_mining_sale_proceeding and sale_process_monitored_by_court_body and (subgrade_ore_commercially_valuable and removal_environmentally_safe)

predicates.court_supervised_mining_sale_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the sale of iron ore connected with mining operations under court supervision.
predicates.sale_process_monitored_by_court_body: A body designated by the Court conducts or monitors the sale process.
predicates.subgrade_ore_commercially_valuable: The sub-grade ore has sufficient commercial value to justify its removal and sale.
predicates.removal_environmentally_safe: Removing the ore is not likely to cause significant environmental harm or destabilize the waste dumps.

issues.definition: When a court-supervised body monitors iron ore sales, those sales may continue, and sub-grade ore may also be sold if it is commercially valuable and can be removed safely.
